title: Human Computer Interaction & AI-Assisted Prototyping
summary: How to design interactive systems around the people who will use them: analysing users, tasks and contexts, structuring information, designing for usability and accessibility, prototyping, and evaluating with experts and with users. In the predecessor CSE3500 this ran as eight lectures, weekly labs on a tourism case and a group project that ended in a report on a controlled user study. CSE12B adds building a software prototype with generative AI and testing it with real users; how it is taught and assessed has not been published.

basis.description: Slides of the eight lectures of the discontinued course CSE3500 Human Computer Interaction (2025 edition, as text), its lab assignments and its official course description. Time shares count text slides; the exam preparation lecture is left out and has no slides in the archive.
basis.caveat: CSE12B is new in the 2026-27 curriculum (year 1, quarter 2). It replaces CSE1500 Web and Database Technology in the curriculum table, but its subject is HCI, so this rests on CSE3500, the closest predecessor. The new part, building a prototype with generative AI and testing it with real users, has no material yet. Lectures 1 to 6 were flipped with videos not in the archive, so slide counts understate them, Lecture 3 most.

topics.name: Usability and the PACT framework
know: Usability as [[effective, efficient and satisfying task completion]] (ISO 9241-11), and how user experience is wider than usability
PACT: [[People, Activities, Contexts and Technologies]], and what each part asks you to describe
People: user characteristics (age, domain and computer experience, frequency of use, freedom of choice, direct or indirect use), novice, occasional and expert users, user classes
Personas and scenarios: a specific person for each core user class, and a short story of how and why they use the system in a given context
Hierarchical task analysis: task and subtask hierarchy, plan types ([[fixed sequence, optional, waiting, cycles, time-sharing, discretionary]]) and refining heuristics
Contexts as [[physical, social and organisational]]; visibility, affordance and perceived affordance as properties of the technology
do: Write a PACT analysis for a short client brief with distinct user groups, activities, contexts and technologies
Build a persona and a scenario for a user class, and draw an HTA with plans for an everyday task
pitfalls: Listing user groups or activities that overlap: the practice marking gives one point per distinct aspect
Putting interface details into tasks and scenarios: the slides keep them interface-free so the same analysis fits a phone, a website or a voice system

topics.name: Requirements and information architecture
know: Requirement elicitation (ethnography, contextual inquiry, interviews, surveys, focus groups) versus analysis (scenarios, task analysis, card sorting)
Information architecture: organising content and designing navigation, shaped by content, context and users
Organisation structures: [[hierarchy (hub and spoke, nested doll), database, linear, hypertext and hybrid]], and when each fits
Exact schemes ([[alphabetical, chronological, geographical]]) versus inexact ones ([[topic, task, audience]]), and the risk of hybrid schemes
Labelling systems that are specific, predictable and consistent; open versus closed card sorting
[[Global, local, contextual and supplemental]] navigation (site map, index, breadcrumbs, search)
do: Choose an organisation structure and scheme for a website or app and defend it
Plan an open or closed card sort and turn its result into a consistent set of labels
Judge whether a survey or focus group plan will give the design team usable input
pitfalls: Mixing kinds of label in one menu, such as a function, a product class and a user group side by side
Choosing labels for reasons the slides reject, such as the space on a button

topics.name: Design principles, UX and research ethics
know: [[Benyon's twelve design principles]] in four groups: learning and remembering (affordance, visibility, familiarity, consistency), being in control (feedback, navigation, control), safety (constraints, recovery) and suitability (style, flexibility, conviviality)
The System Usability Scale: [[ten Likert items, a score out of 100, 68 as the average]], and why comparing systems tells you most
Human research ethics at TU Delft: HREC approval, the risk checklist and mitigation plan
Informed consent: purpose, what participants do, risks including re-identification, mitigation, and [[separate tick boxes per consent point]]
Minimal-risk rules for student studies: no vulnerable groups, no identifiable recordings, no sensitive topics, no deception, anonymised secure storage
do: Name the design principle a described usability problem violates and explain why, using its definition
Spot what is missing or risky in a consent text or study plan and fix it
pitfalls: Picking a nearby principle instead of the closest one: the practice answers want the single best match plus its definition
Bundling several consent points into one yes or no question, which the slides show as a bad example

topics.name: Accessibility and inclusive design
know: Five kinds of exclusion: [[physical, conceptual, economic, cultural and social]], each with a typical example

[[Universal design's seven principles]]: equitable use, use that is flexible, simple and intuitive, information that is perceptible, error tolerance, low physical effort, and enough size and space to approach and use
The guidelines under perceptible information and tolerance for error (redundant modes, contrast, legibility, warnings, fail-safe features)
Inclusivity analysis: a user characteristic is [[fixed or changing, common or rare]], and its solution [[cheap or expensive]]; the tree says whether inclusion is mandatory, recommended or optional
WCAG as the web accessibility standard, and the difference between usable design and inclusive design
do: Classify a described case by type of exclusion
Place a user characteristic in the inclusivity tree and say whether inclusion is required
Give two concrete ways to apply a universal design principle to a given interface
pitfalls: Calling a characteristic fixed when some users have it only part of the time: read the scenario for who has it and when
Answering a universal design question with general usability advice instead of the guidelines of the named principle

topics.name: Envisionment and prototyping
know: A prototype as a [[concrete but partial representation of a design]], and why teams prototype
Fidelity: low (sketches, storyboards, paper, PICTIVE), medium (wireframes, scripted simulations) and high, with the trade-offs of each
[[Horizontal prototypes (the whole surface, little depth)]], [[vertical prototypes (a few features in depth)]] and scenario prototypes (one fixed script)
Throwaway, incremental and evolutionary prototypes
Why low fidelity often beats high fidelity early on: users focus on the big picture and developers stay unattached
Wizard of Oz: [[a hidden human simulates the intelligence]] of a system that does not exist yet
do: Choose the fidelity and kind of prototype for a stage and audience, and justify it
Make a storyboard or wireframe for a scenario from a PACT analysis
pitfalls: Swapping horizontal and vertical: the practice set tests exactly this
Showing a polished prototype too early, so users comment on fonts or think the system already exists

topics.name: Expert evaluation
know: Expert evaluation with usability experts or experts on the users: cheap and quick, but simulated and without real users
Cognitive walkthrough: task, action sequence, anticipated users and goals, and the four questions asked at every step
Heuristic evaluation (Nielsen): experts check the interface on their own against heuristics; it works on paper prototypes
[[Nielsen's ten heuristics]], and the course's twelve design principles used as an alternative list
[[Three to five evaluators]], or until saturation; [[five find about 75 percent of the problems]]
The severity matrix: [[severity set by impact and frequency]], with cost added when choosing what to fix
do: Run a cognitive walkthrough on a login or booking flow and record where users will fail
Give the advantages and disadvantages of heuristic evaluation for a described project
Rate a list of usability problems for severity and choose which to fix first
pitfalls: Forgetting that end users in a participatory heuristic evaluation must first be briefed on the heuristics
Giving a number of evaluators without the reason (diminishing returns or saturation); the reason carries its own point

topics.name: User evaluation and controlled experiments
lectures: Lecture 6 - User Evaluation and Controlled Experiments
know: Research question types (descriptive, comparative, evaluative, defining, explaining, designing) and what makes a question focused, feasible and specific
Qualitative versus quantitative evaluation; cooperative evaluation, think-aloud, co-discovery, interviews and thematic analysis
[[Independent, dependent and confounding variables]]; lab versus field studies
Within-subject versus between-subject and mixed designs, learning effects and counterbalancing
Inclusion and exclusion criteria, sample size and power; subjective (questionnaire), behavioural and physiological measures
Questionnaire quality: [[Cronbach's alpha (0.7 as a rough minimum)]], ceiling effects, reusing validated scales
Significance as a [[false-positive rate below 5 percent]], p-hacking, and why [[a non-significant result does not prove there is no difference]]
do: Design a controlled experiment comparing two versions of a system: question, variables, participants, design, measures, procedure and analysis
Decide between a within-subject and a between-subject design for a given question and explain why
Write the methods section of a user study: participants, procedure, materials, measures, data preparation
pitfalls: Choosing within-subject to save participants when the first condition changes how people do the second; counterbalancing does not remove that
Reading a non-significant difference as evidence that the two conditions are equal

topics.name: Adaptive systems and layered evaluation
know: The five levels of adaptivity (Browne et al.), from changing output on input to reasoning about its own interaction models
Domain models at [[physical, conceptual and intentional level]], and user models
Emotion as discrete categories (Ekman, Plutchik) or as valence and arousal
A Wizard of Oz protocol: what the wizard can observe, what it can do, and how observation leads to action
Layered evaluation: [[collect input, interpret it, model the state of the world, decide on adaptation, apply it]], each with its own criteria
do: Say which layer a described evaluation targets and which criteria fit it
Write a wizard protocol whose action space matches what the real system will be able to do
pitfalls: Letting the wizard observe or do more than the future system could, which makes the results meaningless

topics.name: Conversational interfaces
know: Text, voice and hybrid conversational interfaces, and why they spread: speed, hands-free and screen-free use
Their challenges: high expectations, accents and language, narrow query range, poor discoverability without a GUI
What makes a good conversation ([[common ground, trust, active listening, humour]]) and how people see agent conversations as mostly functional
Conversational styles ([[high involvement versus high considerateness]]) and the research findings on worker engagement
Crowd-powered conversational systems as an extension of Wizard of Oz, their latency and privacy problems, and trust in human-AI interaction
do: Argue for or against a conversational interface for a given task and user group
Describe how you would evaluate a chatbot design with users

prerequisites: Basic statistics helps for the experiment part: mean and standard deviation, significance, t-tests and ANOVA
Comfort writing concise English: the CSE3500 report had a hard word limit
practical: In CSE3500, groups of 4 to 6 ran a project from week 1 to week 9: requirements, design, prototype and a user-centred evaluation, written up in a report of at most 6200 words. It needed at least one controlled experiment with 15 or more participants under minimal-risk ethics rules, and a BuddyCheck peer review. CSE12B's new part, building a software prototype with generative AI and testing it with real users, is not described yet. The archive files the old Web Technology lectures (HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Node.js) under this course as background for building one.
studyAdvice: Learn the fixed lists by heart: the twelve design principles, the seven universal design principles with their guidelines, the five exclusion types, Nielsen's ten heuristics and the four cognitive walkthrough questions. Most practice points ask you to apply them.
Accessibility takes 2 percent of the slides but a whole practice set; the topic was taught mainly through videos. Give it far more time than its slide count suggests.
Practise PACT analyses on any short brief until you can produce distinct user groups, activities, contexts and technologies in a few minutes.
Study controlled experiment design carefully even though no practice question covers it: it is the core of the predecessor's project, and evaluating with real users is the new part of CSE12B.
Conversational interfaces fill 19 percent of the slides, much of it research case studies; learn the main concepts and challenges rather than every study result.
Plan your study for user tests early: in CSE3500 the experiment needed ethics checks and 15 or more participants, and groups had to start right after the experiments lecture.
